steps.prompt: Most viewers watch with the sound OFF. So what keeps them watching?
steps.sub: A wall of static subtitles is easy to ignore. Captions that light up word-by-word, in time with the voice, pull the eye along. By the end you'll know why they boost watch-time — and how to do them right.

steps.prompt: What makes a caption "kinetic" instead of a plain subtitle?

options.t: It's a big block of all the scene's text, shown the whole time.
Each word highlights exactly as it's spoken, so the eye follows the voice in real time.
It's the same subtitle file you'd burn into a DVD.

steps.why: Kinetic = moving with the voice. Instead of a static block you read once and tune out, the current word lights up the instant it's spoken. That live sync is what holds a muted viewer's attention through the whole scene.
hints: A static block you read in one second. A word-by-word highlight you follow for the whole line.

steps.prompt: Why word-synced captions earn their place.
steps.sub: Tap each card. Three reasons they're worth the extra step.

cards.b: On phones, most feeds autoplay silent. Captions ARE your narration for them.
The highlight gives the eye something to track, so people stay through the scene instead of swiping.
Deaf and hard-of-hearing viewers, and anyone in a noisy place, can follow every word.
Timing comes from the narration audio — each word appears exactly when it's said.

steps.prompt: Caption choices: which help retention, which hurt it?
steps.sub: Tap a choice, then the bin.

items.t: Highlighting the current word as it's spoken
Dumping a whole paragraph on screen at once
1–4 words on screen at a time, kept in sync
Tiny text crammed into the very bottom edge

hints: What can a thumb-scrolling viewer actually read in half a second?
If they have to pause and squint, you've lost them. Big, short, synced wins.

steps.prompt: Order the steps to produce word-synced captions.
chips: Generate the narration audio from the script
Get per-word timestamps from the audio
Render captions burned onto the video, synced to those timestamps
hints: You can't time captions to a voice that doesn't exist yet.
Timestamps come from the audio; styling and rendering come after you know the timing.

steps.goal: Produce word-synced captions that hold muted viewers.

options: A different font, picked at random

turns.situation: You have a timestamp for every word. Now you decide how text appears.
turns.q: Which layout holds a muted phone viewer best?
options: The whole sentence as a tiny block, full duration
1–4 big words at a time, the current one highlighted
No captions — the visuals are enough
turns.log: 🔤 Style → 2-3 big words, current word highlighted

turns.q: What's broken, and what fixes it?
options: Bind each word's appearance to its timestamp
Make the font bigger and ignore timing
turns.log: 🔗 Sync → each word lights up as it's spoken

turns.situation: Captions now track the voice perfectly, big and readable.
turns.q: Why does this version keep viewers longer?
options: It gives the eye a moving target and serves the muted majority

hints: The win is a moving highlight that muted viewers can follow word by word.

steps.sub: Tap True or False for each, then check all at once.

statements.t: Captions only matter for accessibility, not for views.
statements.why: False — accessibility is one real reason, but the bigger commercial reason is that most feed views are muted. Captions are your narration for them, and they directly raise retention.

statements.t: Word-by-word highlighting gives the eye a moving target that holds attention.
statements.why: True — a static block gets read once and ignored; a live highlight keeps pulling the eye along with the voice, scene after scene.

statements.t: Caption timing should come from the narration audio.
statements.why: True — per-word timestamps from the audio are what let each word appear exactly when it's spoken. Eyeballing the timing drifts out of sync.

statements.t: Cramming the full paragraph on screen is fine as long as it's readable.
statements.why: False — a wall of text gets skimmed and tuned out. A few big words at a time, synced and highlighted, is what actually holds people.

hints: Think about how YOU watch a feed with the sound off.
Sync comes from the audio; less text on screen reads faster.

steps.prompt: Two creators post the same 30-second tip. One uses static subtitles, one uses word-synced kinetic captions. The kinetic one gets noticeably higher average watch-time. Why?

options.t: Kinetic captions make the audio louder.
The moving highlight keeps muted viewers actively reading instead of swiping away.
The algorithm just prefers fancier effects.

steps.why: It's not magic or volume — it's attention. Most of those views are silent, and a live word-by-word highlight gives the eye a reason to stay on each beat. Static subtitles get glanced at once; kinetic ones are followed the whole way through.
hints: The audio is identical in both. So it's not about sound.
What does a moving highlight do for a viewer who can't hear it?

steps.prompt: Tap ALL the things that make captions boost watch-time.
steps.sub: Some of these feel right but actually drag retention down. Pick only the helpers.
chips: Timing pulled from the narration audio
A few big words at a time
A full paragraph shown at once
Tiny text jammed at the screen edge
steps.why: Retention comes from a live highlight, timing taken from the audio, short bursts of big readable text. A full paragraph or tiny edge text both make viewers skim and swipe.
hints: Recall the cards: muted viewers, retention, accessibility, synced.
If it makes a muted phone viewer squint or stop reading, it hurts watch-time.
